newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Tanzanian telecoms resists moves to privatise.
newsitem.headline: Tanzanian telecoms resists moves to privatise.

text.p: Tanzania's state-owned telecommunications monopoly will be privatised, probably within 12 months, despite opposition from its management, government officials said on Wednesday.
"What has been taking place are meetings to thrash out the best possible divestiture strategy for TTCL," said Vuyo Wagi, public relations officer for the Parastatal Sector Reform Commission.
"We're waiting for a government decision but recommendations have been made," he said.

Wagi told Reuters that recent meetings to discuss the privatisation of Tanzanian Telecommunications Company Limited (TTCL) involved the state-owned Tanzania Communications Commission and the ministry of communications and transport.
He said the final decision on a timetable rested with communications minister William Kusila.
However, senior government officials familiar with the privatisation proposal told Reuters that TTCL's management was strongly resisting moves to sell-off the company.

The officials said government aid from Canada, Britain, Japan and Sweden -- aimed at rehabilitating Tanzania's dilapidated communications sector -- had encouraged TTCL's board to try to "go it alone".

"The government is removing itself from business and TTCL has to prepare itself for this eventuality," one government official said. "If they don't go into the free market and compete they will simply die."
The senior representative of the IMF, Festus Osunsade, said the IMF had no reason to doubt the government's commitment to privatisation.

"As far as TTCL is concerned, under the ESAF (enhanced structural adjustment facility) the government is committed to complete by the end of June, 1997 an invitation for potential buyers to bid," he said.
What potential buyers would be bidding for remains unclear and the IMF has called for an independent audit before privatisation.
The IMF restored ESAF credit to Tanzania following an agreement with the government which included a timetable for privatising scores of state-owned assets.
Despite attempts to modernise, Tanzania's telecoms industry is a model of chronic inefficiancy.

Telephone links with provincial centres are patchy and unreliable. Some diplomats attending a summit on Burundi in the Northern town of Arusha last week were forced to use satellite phones to contact their home bases as land links were so poor.
The ratio of telephone ownership in Tanzania is also low with just one telephone per 100,000 people compared to India's one per 10,000.

However, recently a string of private telecom operators have sprung up and Dar Es Salaam alone boasts eight operators including two mobile phone operators. Most of the others run card-operated call-box networks.
